sources.title: Wikipedia: Correlation does not imply causation

sections.body: Two things are correlated when they tend to change together. That doesn't mean one causes the other.
Confounding variable: a third factor causing both. Ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer. Ice cream doesn't cause drowning. Hot weather increases both swimming and ice-cream buying.
Reverse causation: maybe B causes A, not A causes B. People who exercise more may sleep better, or people who sleep better may have more energy to exercise.
Coincidence: with enough data, some unrelated things will line up by chance.
How scientists test causation: randomised controlled trials. People are randomly assigned to groups so the only systematic difference is the thing being tested.
Find a news headline that says 'X linked to Y'. List one possible confounder and one possible reverse-causation story.

quiz.q: Students who eat breakfast get better grades. What's the best conclusion from this alone?
options: They're correlated; a confounder like home routine could explain it
hints: Is this an experiment or an observation?
What else might differ between students who eat breakfast and those who don't?
Example: 'People with more books at home earn more' — maybe family income affects both.
quiz.explain: From observation alone we only know they're correlated. Factors like family routine or sleep could drive both.

quiz.q: Which study design best tests whether a new study app causes higher test scores?
options: Randomly assign students to use it or not, then compare
Survey students who already use it
hints: How do you rule out other differences between groups?
Who decides which students use the app?
Example: medicine trials randomly give some people the drug and others a placebo.
quiz.explain: Random assignment makes the groups similar in everything except the app, so differences can be attributed to it.

quiz.q: Cities with more police officers have more crime. A likely explanation is…
options: Reverse causation: high-crime cities hire more police
hints: Why would a city decide to hire more police?
Example: hospitals have more sick people than gyms, but hospitals don't cause sickness. Sick people go there.
quiz.explain: Cities with more crime tend to hire more police, so the causal arrow likely runs the other way.
